newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk workers protest march for shipyard rescue.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk workers protest march for shipyard rescue.

text.p: Thousands of workers from the Gdansk shipyard, the birthplace of Solidarity trade union, marched through the city on Wednesday to demand government credit guarantees to save their enterprise from bankrupcy.

The workers want the government to provide guarantees for banks, which would finance the completion of existing contracts to build five ships, while the yard seeks an investor to save the whole business. The government said it was standing firm.

"The government will not give guarantees for the Gdansk shipyard as there is no bank willing to grant credits for the enterprise's further operations," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told reporters in Warsaw.
The treasury and industry ministries are due to hold talks on Thursday on a possible future investor.

So far the ministry has not commented on the only offer sofar, from Laman Poland which represents Norwegian interests and a shipyard in that country. Laman is offering to acquire the yard for $20 million spread over 10 years.
One bank associated with the city, Bank Gdanski, said it was not interested in financing the entire yard, but might consider offering credits for specific shipbuilding projects.

"Bank Gdanski could take part only in a larger effort aimed at getting profits from building ships. This could be a banking consortium supported by the shipyard owners," the bank's spokesman Adam Grzybowski told Reuters.
Three workers went on a hunger strike accepting liquids only, Jerzy Borowczak, the head of the yard's Solidarity branch, told Reuters.

Earlier about 2,000 of the 5,000 employees still working at the yard, where Solidarity arose under Lech Walesa's leadership in 1980 to defy communist rule, marched to the Gdansk municipal government offices shouting slogans such as: "We want work".
Around 300 workers have been occupying the offices since Monday in protest. Borowczak said they would stay overnight.
But he said the union would suspend protest marches until Friday, when the next round of talks with the Treasury Ministry, responsible for state assets, were due to be held.

Cimoszewicz, who heads a cabinet dominated by ex-communists, said the government might reconsider if such a bank were found, but warned the union that if it continued what he called a "politicisation" of the issue it could put off investors.

The union has accused the government of planning to let the state-controlled shipyard sink under its debts in order to destroy a hotbed of opposition. But the government argues that it can not keep subsidising an inefficient company. -- Ryszard Wesolowski +48 22 653 9700
